conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Durham Bulls Athletic Park $10.2 Million MLB Upgrades and Public Accountability (Item 13)
conflicts.summary: Council members split over doubling city funding toward $10.2 million in MLB-mandated Durham Bulls stadium renovations, with Jillian Johnson questioning whether the city should invest further public dollars in a 'money suck' private franchise without full net fiscal-impact accounting, while Middleton, Freeman, and O'Neal argued keeping the Bulls is vital to Durham's brand, downtown economy, and contracts.
conflicts.side_a_position: Withhold automatic Consent approval and require full fiscal-impact, debt-service, and lease-consequence reporting before committing $10M+.
side_a_arguments: Taxpayers already cover substantial debt and maintenance costs while MLB imposes unfunded renovation mandates.
Residents deserve a clear financial ledger comparing stadium costs against direct city revenues before spending another $10 million.
conflicts.side_b_position: Move forward unconditionally to satisfy MLB standards and keep the Durham Bulls franchise in Durham.
side_b_arguments: Losing the franchise would damage Durham's civic identity and downtown hospitality economy, as occurred in Richmond.
Delaying the Skanska bid jeopardizes construction before the 2023-2025 compliance deadlines.
conflicts.resolution: Item 13 was moved to the April 4 General Business Agenda at Johnson's request while staff committed to compiling economic-impact and lease briefs.

conflicts.issue: Procedural Continuance vs. Immediate Vote on Bull City Townhomes Rezoning (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Although all five members ultimately voted against approving the Bull City Townhomes rezoning over unfinalized proffers, neighborhood engagement failures, and watershed/traffic concerns, members split over whether to grant applicant Mark Bullock another continuance until August.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to August to give the applicant another opportunity to formalize proffers and address neighborhood engagement.
side_a_arguments: Freeman cited Jordan Lake buffer concerns and unresolved community outreach while asking to continue to August.
Johnson supported townhome density in principle and said she was open to a continuance if proffers were solidified.
conflicts.side_b_position: Refuse a fourth continuance because the applicant had already had multiple meetings and did not commit to meaningful changes.
side_b_arguments: Middleton argued another continuance would set a bad precedent when the applicant indicated another meeting would not yield new outcomes.
Letting the applicant reapply later is cleaner than keeping neighbors in repeated hearing loops.
conflicts.resolution: Freeman's continuance motion died for lack of a second, and the Council voted 0-5 to deny the rezoning.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: ARPA Allocation Framework, 50% Funding Cap, and Black-Led Organization Focus
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over ground rules for the upcoming April 6 ARPA deliberation, specifically whether a circulated spreadsheet cutting County-function health proposals and capping initial awards at ~50% ($22M) of the $44M ARPA balance reflected Council consensus.
conflicts.side_a_position: Use the staff-vetted spreadsheet cutoff to release roughly half (~$22M) immediately for urgent community aid while reserving half for larger equity investments or county partnerships.
side_a_arguments: Avoids stalling urgent community funds and relies on staff scoring without re-reading 77 full RFPs.
Preserves ~$22M unencumbered for transformative equity projects or joint County health/wellness funding.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not pre-lock a 50% cap or exclude proposals prematurely without a broader strategic plan and explicit Black-led/Black-focused equity prioritization.
side_b_arguments: Freeman stated she had not agreed to a $22M cap and wanted a larger comprehensive strategy.
Council must explicitly confirm prioritization of Black-led and Black-focused proposals rather than assuming scoring suffices.
conflicts.resolution: Mayor O'Neal tasked Caballero and Williams with designing a structured April 6 deliberation and public comment framework bounded by staff cutoff tiers and explicit equity attention.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Boards and Commissions In-Person Return and Attendance Enforcement Policy
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over whether advisory and quasi-judicial boards and commissions (such as Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment) should be directed to return in person with attendance enforcement restored, or remain remote until the Governor ends North Carolina's COVID-19 State of Emergency.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require business-critical boards and commissions to meet in person and restore attendance accountability now, accommodating immunocompromised members individually.
side_a_arguments: Freeman argued Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment work is backing up because landlords and participants avoid virtual proceedings.
Williams advocated leading by example with masks, vaccines, and boosters to return boards to in-person work, though clarifying later he meant once the Governor's emergency order lifts.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep existing virtual meeting flexibility and suspended attendance penalties in place until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency.
side_b_arguments: Johnson warned toggling between in-person and virtual rules during future COVID spikes would confuse volunteers and strain staff.
City Attorney Kim Rehberg cautioned that City Hall lacks hybrid equipment outside Council Chambers and piecemeal board autonomy could create chaos.
conflicts.resolution: Council maintained the virtual/non-counted attendance status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 7, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Affordable Housing RFP Scoring Transparency and Council Oversight Role (Items 5-9)
conflicts.summary: Following public complaints from Geer Street Residential representatives over rejected development loan applications and lack of RFP scoring feedback, Council Member DeDreana Freeman pushed City Manager Wanda Page for clearer scoring transparency and equity guardrails for local/community developers, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton cautioned against council intervention in staff procurement appeals.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require stronger RFP scoring transparency and equity guardrails so local/nonprofit housing developers understand and trust award outcomes.
side_a_arguments: Unexplained RFP rejections breed distrust among local community housing developers.
Council must ensure scoring rubrics include clear equity guardrails before projects advance.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain strict staff insulation in procurement scoring while formal protest appeals proceed through administrative channels.
side_b_arguments: Referring Items 5 and 6 back to Community Development protects the integrity of the pending appeal.
Council members should avoid adjudicating technical RFP scoring during live procurement disputes.
conflicts.resolution: Items 5 and 6 remained referred back pending administrative appeal resolution, while Items 7-9 stayed on Consent.

meetings.executive_summary: In the full-audio recording of the May 5, 2022 Durham City Council Work Session, all six seated members attended as Council recognized AAPI Heritage Month, reminded residents of early voting ahead of the May 17 primary, and celebrated Durham's NC League of Municipalities 'Most Entrepreneurial City' award for Innovate Durham. City Manager Wanda Page introduced six priority items, including rule-suspension requests for JFK Towers and Cedar Terrace Apartments affordable housing loan commitments alongside strategic youth, water/sewer rate, FY23 budget/CIP, and stormwater rate items. meetings.title: Special Durham City Council May 3, 2022 at 6 p.m. Council Vacancy Public Comment (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: On May 3, 2022, the Durham City Council held a special public comment meeting with all six seated members present to hear community input on the four finalists for the vacant At-Large Council seat: Nate Baker, Shaniqua Nicole Diggs, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and Henry McCoy Jr. Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the meeting and turned presiding duties over to Legislative Committee Co-Chair Jillian Johnson, who allotted 30 minutes of speaking time per candidate in alphabetical order. In the portions captured by the digest, speakers supporting Nate Baker highlighted his Planning Commission service, Braggtown advocacy, and mastery of the Unified Development Ordinance and Comprehensive Plan on affordable housing and growth, while supporters of Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. emphasized his national inclusive economic development work, Helius entrepreneurship initiatives, and cross-community bridge building. No formal votes were taken, and Mayor O'Neal adjourned the session at 7:59 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Presiding Handoff, Ground Rules, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal welcomed residents in chambers and online to the Council vacancy public comment session for the four finalists and invited Legislative Committee Co-Chair Jillian Johnson to preside. Johnson outlined the format granting 30 minutes per finalist's supporters in alphabetical order (Nate Baker, Shaniqua Nicole Diggs, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and Henry McCoy Jr.), and the Clerk confirmed all six seated Council members were present.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of At-Large Finalist Nate Baker
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Virtual and in-person supporters—beginning with Braggtown resident Celeste Ritchie and environmental/planning advocates—urged Council to appoint Nate Baker. Speakers emphasized his urban planning expertise, grassroots work encouraging proactive developer engagement in Braggtown, and command of Durham's Unified Development Ordinance and Comprehensive Plan in addressing affordable housing and intense development pressures.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of At-Large Finalist Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters of Dr. Henry McCoy Jr.—including a Harvard adjunct professor whose inclusive economic development guide co-developed with McCoy was adopted by the Biden administration's OMB, Matt Kopac, and local partners—highlighted McCoy's entrepreneurship training via Helius and his ability to unify Black, Latino, and business communities. Council Member Johnson thanked all applicants and residents before Mayor O'Neal adjourned the special meeting at 7:59 p.m.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council May 2, 2022 at 3 p.m. Council Vacancy Interviews (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal convened a special Durham City Council meeting on May 2, 2022, with all six seated members present (Elaine O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams), and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton facilitated questioning as Procedures Committee chair for the four finalists seeking the at-large seat vacated by Charlie Reece. Council interviewed urban planner Nate Baker, North Carolina Central University public administration professor Dr. Nicole Diggs, social work educator and DSS Board Vice Chair Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and former North Carolina Assistant Secretary of Commerce Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. Questioning focused on Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) reform and small-area planning, affordable housing strategies, support for the Community Safety Department and unarmed crisis response versus traditional policing, economic equity and small-business growth, local voting engagement, and potential conflict-of-interest optics regarding Dr. McCoy's uncompensated advisory work with Hayti Reborn on Durham Housing Authority matters. No formal motions or votes were taken during the interview session, which concluded with Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton announcing a May 3 public comment hearing at 6:00 p.m. and a Council appointment vote scheduled for the Thursday work session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Finalist Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the special meeting to order at 3:00 p.m. and directed the City Clerk to call the roll, confirming all six seated members (Elaine O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams) were present. Mayor O'Neal introduced the finalists present for the at-large seat vacated by Charlie Reece before Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton assumed facilitation on behalf of the Procedures Committee.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Nate Baker
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Urban planner and four-year Durham Planning Commission member Nate Baker identified gun violence, traffic fatalities caused by car-dependent design, and rapid growth/displacement as Durham's top challenges. He advocated a comprehensive rewrite of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), proactive small-area and corridor planning linked to Engaged Durham, and continued investment in the Community Safety Department while stating he did not favor defunding the police. During follow-up questioning, Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman challenged his suggestion that Durham lacked small-area planning, citing the Ninth Street Compact Design District.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Nicole Diggs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NCCU assistant professor of public administration Dr. Nicole Diggs emphasized housing affordability, rental and down-payment assistance, pacing development with 80%, 60%, and 30% AMI set-asides, workforce alignment for incoming tech jobs, and unarmed alternatives to policing. DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned her local voting history, and Dr. Diggs explained she had remained registered in Virginia until recently voting in North Carolina the prior Thursday. Jillian Johnson also asked Dr. Diggs to clarify she was not formally declaring a future candidacy during the broadcast to avoid triggering campaign committee filing deadlines.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Social work professor and Durham County DSS Board Vice Chair Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman outlined her background in intensive case management, family preservation, and grassroots social services. She prioritized community safety, youth programming, expanded reentry support before release, developer 'pay-to-play' housing affordability expectations alongside financial literacy rather than temporary subsidies alone, ShotSpotter technology, and a proposed 'community safety intensive case management mobile crisis unit' pairing social workers, medical/mental health staff, and peer support.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Henry McCoy Jr.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Former NC Assistant Secretary of Commerce and faculty member Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. centered his remarks on 'equity by design,' leveraging public land, inclusionary zoning, impact-investor partnerships to connect residents to economic growth without displacement, and expanding unarmed crisis and traffic response. Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman pressed Dr. McCoy on potential conflict-of-interest optics regarding his advocacy for the Hayti Reborn proposal before the Durham Housing Authority (DHA); Dr. McCoy stated on the record that he held no equity stake, was not a paid consultant, and had no financial interest in the project.

agenda_items.title: Procedures Housekeeping and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton thanked all four finalists and announced that public comment on the vacancy finalists would be held on May 3, 2022 at 6:00 p.m., followed by a Council appointment vote at the Thursday work session. He yielded back to Mayor Elaine O'Neal, who adjourned the special meeting at 03:02:08 ahead of the 7:00 p.m. regular meeting.

meetings.title: Joint City Council - DHA Board Meeting April 11, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council and the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board of Commissioners held a virtual special joint informational meeting to review Forever Home Durham investments, DHA's operational stabilization, and HUD Troubled Agency Recovery Agreement obligations. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson detailed $160 million in city affordable housing commitments including $59 million in bond funds for the first four Downtown Durham Neighborhood Plan (DDNP) phases and $4.5 million for non-DDNP repairs at McDougald Terrace, Laurel Oaks, and Morreene Road. DHA CEO Anthony Scott reported progress cutting work-order backlogs from 1,600 to under 13 and reducing Fresh Start eviction risks, while explaining HUD mandates requiring 95% occupancy, a REAC score of 60 or higher by June 30, 2023, and repositioning McDougald Terrace out of public housing within two years. No formal votes were taken, though Council members and public residents raised sharp questions about McDougald Terrace preservation, right-to-return protections under RAD conversions, and holding regular quarterly joint meetings.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks and Joint Council-DHA Board Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DHA Board Chair Dan Hudgins opened the 1:00 PM virtual joint session with introductions from seated City Council members (O'Neal, Middleton, Caballero, Freeman, with Johnson joining during the meeting and Williams absent out of town) and DHA Commissioners (Hudgins, Vice Chair Mimi Webb Bledsoe, Christine Westfall, Bo Glenn, Terrell Armstrong, Pebbles Lucas, and Angela Holmes). Participants emphasized strengthening formal communication between the City and DHA after past tensions and crises.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham Affordable Housing and Forever Home Durham Partnership Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the City's $160 million Forever Home Durham capital framework combining the $95 million affordable housing bond, dedicated two-cent housing tax funds, and HUD grants. He highlighted $59 million in bond funds committed to the first four DDNP redevelopment phases, $4.5 million for urgent non-DDNP repairs across McDougald Terrace, Laurel Oaks, and Morreene Road, $2.7 million in operations and relocation support, and homelessness coordination delivering 225 Housing Choice Vouchers and 68 Emergency Housing Vouchers.

agenda_items.title: DHA CEO Anthony Scott Comprehensive Operations, HUD Recovery Agreement, and DDNP Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA CEO Anthony Scott reported serving over 4,000 families (9,200+ residents) amid 33% staff vacancies and 35% turnover, while cutting >30-day work-order backlogs from 1,600 to fewer than 13 through a centralized call line. He reviewed DHA's February 2022 HUD Recovery Agreement resulting from its 2018 PHAS score of 59, requiring 95% occupancy and a REAC score >=60 by June 30, 2023 (or third-party management) plus a repositioning plan for McDougald Terrace due February 2023 given a preliminary $53 million 20-year capital need. Scott and staff also updated redevelopment at JJ Henderson, The Joyce (80 senior units), Liberty Street/East Main phases (Elizabeth Street and Commerce Street), Phase II RFP planning for DHA headquarters, Fayette Place, and Forest Hill Heights, Fresh Start rent-arrears relief, and ConnectHome Wi-Fi, while taking tough questions from residents Jacqueline Wagstaff and Mr. Robertson about McDougald Terrace and Lincoln Apartments.

agenda_items.title: Joint Policy Discussion, Public Chat Q&A, and Quarterly Meeting Cadence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed Scott to clarify for residents what HUD's phrase 'repositioning out of public housing inventory' means under RAD and Section 18 (preserving subsidies and right-to-return guarantees) and asked how work orders are closed out. Council members addressed public chat inquiries from Raquel Williams-Jones and Sonia Laurie regarding Jobs Plus outreach, Section 3 contracting, and RAD resident council organizing rights, and Council and DHA Board leaders agreed to pursue quarterly joint meetings.

disagreements.side_a_position: Withhold automatic Consent approval and require full fiscal-impact, debt-service, and lease-consequence reporting before committing $10M+.

disagreements.issue: ARPA Allocation Framework, 50% Funding Cap, and Black-Led Organization Focus
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over ground rules for the upcoming April 6 ARPA deliberation, specifically whether a circulated spreadsheet cutting County-function health proposals and capping initial awards at ~50% ($22M) of the $44M ARPA balance reflected Council consensus.
disagreements.side_a_position: Use the staff-vetted spreadsheet cutoff to release roughly half (~$22M) immediately for urgent community aid while reserving half for larger equity investments or county partnerships.
side_a_arguments: Avoids stalling urgent community funds and relies on staff scoring without re-reading 77 full RFPs.
Preserves ~$22M unencumbered for transformative equity projects or joint County health/wellness funding.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 21, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all six seated members present, the City Council passed the Consent Agenda unanimously 6-0, including Durham City-County Appearance Commission appointments, the 2021 ASOC report, a Gang Reduction Strategy interlocal agreement, and Braggtown sidewalk funding. During a well-attended FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 CIP public hearing, residents urged equity-based CIP investments, eviction diversion, DOST open space staffing, and rejection of the ShotSpotter pilot, while Council Members Leonardo Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voiced strong defense of evaluating a guarded ShotSpotter trial. Following an extensive rezoning hearing on the 134-acre Carver Street Assemblage (up to 821 homes including 198 affordable units), Council Member Freeman raised Cub Creek infrastructure concerns with NCDOT, and Council unanimously approved 6-0 annexation, utility extension, PDR zoning, and consistency statements. The Council concluded by conducting a quasi-judicial hearing and unanimously voting 6-0 to grant TROSA a Major Special Use Permit and Major Site Plan expanding its James Street residential capacity from 275 to 450.

agenda_items.title: March for Meals Proclamation, NLC Announcements, and Consent Agenda (Items 1-7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero presented a March for Meals proclamation to Meals on Wheels Durham Executive Director Jason Peace, and council members recapped National League of Cities advocacy in Washington, D.C. With no pulls, Council unanimously passed Consent Items 1-7 by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 Capital Improvement Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore opened the initial FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 CIP hearing (comment remaining open until June 21). Speakers Stella Adams (equity CIP scoring for Braggtown, Walltown, Southside, and NE Central Durham), Hibo and DOST Chair Laura Stroud (open space implementer FTE and $100k fund), Larissa Sybel ($6M eviction diversion and local vouchers), Angela Vick Lewis (hotel-to-home/shelters), and Bike Durham's John Tallmadge and Austin Harper (fare-free transit and capital delivery) outlined budget priorities, while Danette Wilkins and Brittany Price urged rejecting ShotSpotter. In response, Council Members Williams and Middleton strongly defended testing a guarded ShotSpotter gunshot-detection pilot, while Freeman endorsed equity CIP funding, DOST staffing, and homelessness support.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Public hearing remains open)

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning: Carver Street Assemblage (KLA Development Co.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Alexander Cahill presented a consolidated voluntary annexation and rezoning for ~134 acres along Carver Street and Old Oxford Road from RS-20 and RU-5 to PDR 7.000 F/J-B for up to 821 residences (single-family, townhomes, and apartments including 198 4% LIHTC units) with 22% tree save, 150-foot stream buffers, and $2 million in infrastructure commitments. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and Braggtown Community Association leaders including Vanessa Mason-Evans spoke in support, while Cub Creek Road residents (represented by Matthew Council and neighbors including Rebecca Painter, Lalit Yadav, and Onofrio Castiglia) objected to unpaved state-maintained Cub Creek conditions and well-water impacts rather than housing affordability. Assistant Transportation Director Bill Judge explained southern Cub Creek lies outside annexation limits, and Council approved annexation, rezoning, and consistency statements 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (3 votes: annexation/utility agreement, zoning map change, consistency statement)

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing: TROSA Main Campus Expansion (1820 James Street)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council conducted a sworn quasi-judicial hearing on TROSA's Major Special Use Permit and Major Site Plan requests to consolidate operations from North Street onto its 13.2-acre James Street campus, increasing residential capacity from 275 to 450 residents and adding ~55,000 square feet including a new dormitory. Planner Robin Schultz, applicant counsel Patrick Byker, former Mayors Bill Bell and Nick Tennyson, Tuscaloosa-Lakewood Neighborhood Association President Grant Gardner, and expert witnesses entered Exhibits A-E into the record without opposition. Council approved both the Major SUP and Major Site Plan 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (2 votes: Major SUP and Major Site Plan)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The six seated Council members approved City Manager priority updates 6-0 and engaged in pointed scrutiny during presentations on the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail (GTCR) Study and the Durham County Transit Plan update. Council Member Leonardo Williams, Mayor Elaine O'Neal, and Council Member Javiera Caballero pressed GoTriangle CEO Chuck Lattuca for an itemized breakdown of the $157 million spent on the canceled light rail project, clearer accounting on the $9 million commuter rail study, and direct City Council voting governance rather than relying on an advisory August support letter. Council also received public comment on recovery housing, reviewed pulled consent items on Appearance Commission gender diversity and Moss+Ross outreach, and established a vacancy timeline opening at-large applications March 11-25 ahead of May 2 interviews and a May 3 final vote. On boards and commissions rules, members split over returning to in-person mandatory attendance immediately versus retaining the remote status quo until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency before settling the March 21 agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Board Attendance Bylaw Referral, and Citizen Matters (Divine Trust Ministries)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested technical updates to Consent Item 5 (Gang Reduction Strategy ILA attachments) and Item 9 (Transit Plan slide 7), which Council approved 6-0 on roll call. City Clerk Diana Schreiber raised reverting boards and commissions to pre-COVID attendance rules (deferred to Other Matters), and resident Andrew McDonald of Divine Trust Ministries appealed for recovery housing support.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Appearance Commission (Item 1) and Moss+Ross Communications Contract (Item 4)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Jillian Johnson pulled Item 1 to recommend re-advertising a vacant Appearance Commission seat to improve gender balance after two male nominees advanced, gaining informal thumbs-up consensus. Council Members Leonardo Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton discussed Item 4 with staff, focusing on print/mail reach and expanding NCCU/university community engagement under the Moss+Ross contract amendment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Informal consensus to re-advertise 1 seat

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail (GTCR) Feasibility Study Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle President and CEO Chuck Lattuca, STV consultant Mariah Ellington, and GoTriangle staff briefed Council on Phase 2 commuter rail alternatives—comparing low-level Concept 2 (+$15M estimated capital) and high-level Concept D (+$35M), operating speeds, and 18-mile vs 43-mile service horizons—noting Durham would only be asked for a non-binding support letter around August. Council Members Williams, Freeman, Caballero, and Mayor O'Neal challenged GoTriangle's lack of project cost breakdowns, Durham's lack of a direct seat on the transit plan voting structure despite generating ~80% of transit activity, and unresolved questions over the $157 million spent on the canceled Durham-Orange Light Rail project.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Durham County Transit Plan Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO Transportation Planning Manager Aaron Cain outlined financial updates to the 20-year Durham County Transit Plan, noting rising GoTriangle (7.4%) and GoDurham (20.5%) operator/fuel cost pressures, a $10 million revenue reserve, a $1.95 billion commuter rail capital placeholder, and an unresolved funding gap depending on whether non-federal local share settles at 20% ($388M) or 33% ($649M). Council members discussed revising the 2013 interlocal governance agreement, securing federal infrastructure grants, and organizing public education ahead of May public release.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Council Vacancy Schedule, Board Remote Attendance Policy, and Set March 21 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton clarified that North Carolina statute does not strictly enforce a 60-day penalty clock on filling Charlie Reece's seat and won consensus for a timeline opening applications March 11-25, distributing packets March 28, picking finalists April 7, conducting interviews May 2 at 4:00 PM, and holding public comment and voting May 3 at 6:00 PM. Council then debated whether to enforce pre-COVID in-person board attendance rules immediately before opting to retain the virtual status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order, and voted 6-0 to settle the March 21 agenda.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Items (Updated Attachments on Item 5 and Item 9)
votes.discussion_detail: Revises attachments on Gang Reduction Strategy ILA and Durham County Transit Plan update.

votes.item_title: Set Agenda for March 21, 2022 City Council Meeting
votes.discussion_detail: Sets Consent Items 1-7 and GBA Public Hearings 10-12 for the March 21 regular meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Boards and Commissions In-Person Return and Attendance Enforcement Policy
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over whether advisory and quasi-judicial boards and commissions (such as Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment) should be directed to return in person with attendance enforcement restored, or remain remote until the Governor ends North Carolina's COVID-19 State of Emergency.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require business-critical boards and commissions to meet in person and restore attendance accountability now, accommodating immunocompromised members individually.
side_a_arguments: Freeman argued Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment work is backing up because landlords and participants avoid virtual proceedings.
Williams advocated leading by example with masks, vaccines, and boosters to return boards to in-person work, though clarifying later he meant once the Governor's emergency order lifts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep existing virtual meeting flexibility and suspended attendance penalties in place until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency.
side_b_arguments: Johnson warned toggling between in-person and virtual rules during future COVID spikes would confuse volunteers and strain staff.
City Attorney Kim Rehberg cautioned that City Hall lacks hybrid equipment outside Council Chambers and piecemeal board autonomy could create chaos.
disagreements.resolution: Council maintained the virtual/non-counted attendance status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order.
